children.text:
It depends on what the tasks are. Text-native work like programming or interacting with a terminal should be a lot more immediate for LLMs than something abstract like Starcraft, DOTA, Minecraft or Mindustry. LLMs certainly know the rules for these games, but processing game state and formulating a plan in the form of a Python script or MCP call is a rough debugging loop.

Minecraft is really the perfect example, because humans get all sorts of unfair advantages. Even a young player has enough spatial reasoning to recognize and remember landmarks, visualize large projects or explore without getting lost. These are simple instincts that LLMs will struggle to match even with huge context sizes and native multimodal input.

children.text: it seems to me that would only be true if the amount of knowledge needed to complete a task far exceeds the context limit. Why would that be the case? I find most people are using horribly inefficient contexts, and a naive approach to dark factories/software eng swarms seems to only compound this

If agents are differentiated solely by system instructions (persona and focus) while sharing identical models / similar model capabilities and contexts, I agree the architectural value is minimal.

However, a multi-agent system (MAS) utilizing true separation of concerns, where each agent is equipped with highly scoped tool access, isolated knowledge bases (RAG), and defined operational constraints, significantly optimizes accuracy, latency, and token consumption.

In the referenced example, the agents share identical capabilities, toolsets, and context windows. As a result, there is no functional role differentiation, rendering the multi-agent architecture redundant.

In my experience, you can just give each agent access to the full set of tools (including RAG search) in the form of documentation and skills, and they'll use that efficiently. Skills have a tiny front matter and hardly bloat the context, and the documentation just needs to be tree-structured with cross-links for progressive disclosure. children.author: dantillberg
children.text:
> help you play a video game

I have a similar hobby, and for me it's not so much "helping to play" the original game, but playing a _different_ game, a much richer/strategic game.

It's similar to car racing: most people just drive to get places, and there's little point tuning a car & driver to go fast. But if you want to go fast, then you want to go fast. There are negative externalities, for which it's important to keep the scale in mind, but these hobbies also push the envelope of what we as humans can do.

Excuse the bluntness but...why ?

Might be old inside, but paying and using that many controversial resources (ram, data center space, water, etc.) to help you play a video game ? And you would like to just...talk to it ? Oof. Luddite life might be for me.

I have been "playing" Graveyard Keeper 2 with AI (Claude Max) and I had a blast, it's really a new way to enjoy the game. My approach is a 3-tiered architecture:

- There is a mod (bot) in the game that handles the fast decisions on sub 1-second timescale; it is also hot-reloadable and gives informational overlay.

- There is a decision/policy server that makes macro decisions, such as what to build and what goals to pursue. It knows all the game rules and connects to the mod.

- Finally, AI agent (Claude) connects via MCP to the server. Through it, the micro and macro agents are developed. Both micro and macro policy agents can record what's happening, and the decisions, I usually only use AI to give policy feedback on what could be improved, and for writing the code.

Eventually, the plan is to make the goal planning macro server generic (I call it "game resource planning system", ERP for games) for many games (right now, my top list is Stardew Valley, Factorio and modded Minecraft), with rules (and agents mods/micro policy scripts) available as plugins.

I think it's a great setup because it saves lot of tokens spend on mundane things. (One thing that would make it nicer would be voice support for Claude Code, so I could watch the game and chat with CC what could be done better, without having to read/write.)

children.text: The AI agents have access to a huge bucket of hints implicitly from their training data, no?

Well.  If you give humans no instructions and play Minecraft without any hints, they probably would do what the AI agents did.  Humans, though, realize the game is artificial and has nothing to do with real life... therefore, they go onto Discord, watch Youtube channels, and read about the artificial game rules imposed by Minecraft.  They would prioritize building a shelter (from zombies-skeletons at night) and building an underground well-lit farm.  Minecraft's says crops can grow underground from torches that stay lit forever and that you can create a never-ending source of water by making a 2x2 well and pouring water into it.   In other words, the AI Agents would have played better if they were told to go read some strategy articles about surviving the first few days at Minecraft.

In all this excellent experiment and in the comments here, I can't help but wonder: minecraft is a game made by humans, for humans to play, and it's about (blocky) humans ("of the humans, by the humans, for the humans")

And it seems the AIs weren't so very effective at playing it, at least initially.

So what kind of game would AIs make for themselves to play?
